414.title: Pleasant places (Psalm 16)
414.hook: the lines are fallen to me in pleasant places
414.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 16 in daily prayer, and many churches read it at Easter, following Peter's sermon in Acts 2, which hears it as a psalm of resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm eight, under the moon and stars. Your line was what are we, that you care? Did you look up? Day four hundred fourteen.

Picture a surveyor in ancient Israel, out in the hills with a long cord. When the tribes came into the land, the land was divided by lot, and then measured out with ropes: this field is yours, that slope is your cousin's. Where your lines fell, that was your share, your inheritance, for good. Some families got rich valley soil. Some got rocky hillsides. Some, the priestly tribe of Levi, got no land at all. God told them, I am your portion. And a psalm-writer, looking at his own life, uses that picture: the measuring lines have fallen for me. And he says where they fell.
screen: `A SURVEYOR WITH A CORD.` → `WHERE YOUR LINES FELL.` → `SOME GOT NO LAND AT ALL.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage." Just before that, he names what his share actually is: "The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup." Like the Levites. His real allotment isn't a field. It's God. And so wherever the lines fall, the place is pleasant. The psalm is honest that this is a choice of attention, not a lucky break. "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." Set, as in placed on purpose, the way you'd put a photo on your desk where you'll see it. And the result is joy, even in the body: my heart is glad, my flesh will rest in hope. Then the psalm reaches further than anyone expects. Thou wilt not leave my soul in the grave. And it ends: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore." Christians have heard that ending as resurrection. In the book of Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter quotes this very psalm in the first Christian sermon, and says it speaks of Jesus, whose body did not stay in the grave. One honest note. The psalm's heading calls it a michtam of David, and nobody is sure what michtam means. A golden poem, a secret, an inscription: scholars have guessed. The sources don't settle it. What the psalm does say clearly is that a life can be measured out in rocky hills and still be a goodly heritage, if God is the portion.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY PORTION.` · `I HAVE SET THE LORD BEFORE ME.` · `THE PATH OF LIFE, FULNESS OF JOY.` · `MICHTAM: NOBODY'S SURE.` · then, large: `THE LINES ARE FALLEN UNTO ME IN PLEASANT PLACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one pleasant place in your life. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your lines have fallen. Not the whole map, just one place. A kitchen where people laugh. A walk you take. A friendship. A job, or a corner of one, that you're good at. A chair by a window. Picture it clearly, the light and the sounds. Let yourself say, quietly, this is mine, and it's good. If some of your lines fell on rocky ground, you don't have to pretend otherwise. Just find one pleasant place. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Pleasant places. In Psalm sixteen, where the measuring lines of a life have fallen, when God is its portion.
Your line: a goodly heritage. Today, go to your pleasant place, or tell someone about it, and say thank you for it. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: The heavens declare (Psalm 19)
415.hook: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey
415.howItsDone: Many preachers say the last verse of Psalm 19 before a sermon, and Christians pray the psalm in daily prayer; Haydn's oratorio The Creation sets its opening as a chorus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm sixteen: the measuring lines fell in pleasant places. Your line was a goodly heritage. Where's your pleasant place? Day four hundred fifteen.

Sunrise doesn't make a sound. Neither does a sunset, or the moon coming up orange over a parking lot, or a thunderhead building on a summer afternoon. And yet people stop their cars for these things. They pull out their phones. They nudge whoever is next to them: look. Something is being said, and everyone seems to get it, in every language, without a single word. A poet in ancient Israel noticed that too. And then, halfway through his poem, he made a turn that readers still talk about. He turned from the sky to a book.
screen: `SUNRISE MAKES NO SOUND.` → `EVERYONE SAYS: LOOK.` → `FROM THE SKY TO A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Psalm nineteen opens, in the King James Bible: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the message to the next, like a relay. Then a paradox. The King James reads, "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." But the Hebrew is even stranger. Literally, it says something like: no speech, no words, their voice is not heard. And yet, the next verse says, their line has gone out through all the earth. The sky speaks without saying anything. It's heard everywhere precisely because it uses no words. Then the sun comes out of its tent like a bridegroom, like a runner glad to run its course, and nothing is hidden from its heat. And then, the turn. Without warning, the poem moves from the sun to the law of the LORD, which is perfect, and restores the soul. Of God's judgments the psalm says, "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb." Why put the sky and the law in one poem? Many readers think that's the whole point. God speaks two ways: wordlessly, through everything that's made, and in words, through scripture. Nothing is hid from the sun's heat, the psalm says; and the law, it says, restores the soul. Joseph Haydn set the opening to music in his oratorio The Creation, and the psalm's last line is one many preachers still say before they begin: "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer."
screen: `DAY HANDS THE MESSAGE TO DAY.` · `NO WORDS, YET HEARD EVERYWHERE.` · `THE SUN, LIKE A BRIDEGROOM.` · `SWEETER THAN HONEY.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the sky for a minute. Go to a window or step outside if you can. Look up, and don't name anything. Not the cloud type, not the weather, not the time. Just watch. Notice the light. The color. How fast or slow things are moving up there. Let it say whatever it's saying, without words. Then bring one sentence back in, the psalm's last line, if you pray: let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight. The bell holds the time.
The heavens declare. Psalm nineteen: the sky speaks God's glory without words, and scripture speaks in words, sweeter than honey.
Your line: day unto day, speech. Today, catch one sunrise, sunset or sky, and let it say something to you before you say anything about it. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: My God, my God (Psalm 22)
416.hook: a cry of abandonment that turns to praise; Jesus prayed its first line on the cross
416.howItsDone: Many churches read Psalm 22 on Good Friday, and in some traditions the altar is stripped on Maundy Thursday while it is said or sung; Christians also pray its first line in times of grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heavens declaring God's glory without a word. Your line was day unto day, speech. What did the sky say to you? Day four hundred sixteen.

Some days the psalms are sunrises and pleasant places. Today's isn't. Today's begins in the dark, with a sentence many people have said, or wanted to say, in a hospital corridor, at a graveside, at three in the morning when the prayers seem to hit the ceiling and fall back down. It's the opening of Psalm twenty-two. And the reason it's so famous is not only what it says. It's who said it, centuries after it was written, hanging on a Roman cross outside Jerusalem, near the end.
screen: `TODAY BEGINS IN THE DARK.` → `PRAYERS THAT HIT THE CEILING.` → `WHO SAID IT, ON A CROSS.`

segments.voice: The psalm begins, in the King James Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not a polite complaint. A howl. And notice it still says my God, twice. Even the cry of abandonment is addressed to God. The psalmist doesn't walk away. He shouts toward the One who seems absent. Then the psalm gets very physical. Surrounded by enemies like bulls and dogs. Bones out of joint. A tongue stuck to the jaw. "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." Christians have long been struck by how closely this psalm matches the crucifixion: the mocking crowd, the thirst, the soldiers gambling for Jesus' clothes, which the Gospels describe. And Matthew and Mark both record that near the end, Jesus cried out the first line, in Aramaic: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christians read that cry in more than one way. Many hear real anguish: Jesus entering the deepest human darkness, the feeling of being forsaken, so that no one is ever alone in it again. Many also notice that in his time, quoting the first line of a psalm could call the whole psalm to mind. And the whole psalm doesn't end in the dark. Around verse twenty-two it turns: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee." The cry becomes a song, and by the end, the psalm reaches the ends of the earth and generations not yet born. Both readings hold. The cry is real. And it isn't the last word of the psalm.
screen: `MY GOD, TWICE, EVEN IN THE DARK.` · `GARMENTS PARTED, LOTS CAST.` · `ELI, ELI, LAMA SABACHTHANI.` · `THE CRY TURNS TO PRAISE.` · then, large: `MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the first line honestly. Settle, and breathe. If there's something in your life right now that feels like abandonment, a loss, a silence, an unanswered prayer, let it come up. You don't have to tidy it. If you pray, you can say the first line, slowly, and mean it: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Notice you're still saying my God. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing honestly, out loud or inside, without pretending it's fine. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
My God. The first words of Psalm twenty-two, a cry of abandonment that still calls God mine, and that Jesus prayed on the cross.
Your line: even he cried this. Today, if someone tells you they feel forsaken, don't hurry them out of it. Sit with them in the first line. Day four hundred sixteen.

417.title: Whom shall I fear? (Psalm 27)
417.hook: the Lord is my light; one thing I ask, to dwell in his house
417.howItsDone: Christians often pray Psalm 27 in times of fear and in daily prayer; in Jewish practice it is recited daily from the start of the month of Elul through the autumn festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm twenty-two: My God, my God, a cry that still says my God, and turns to praise. Your line was even he cried this. Did you sit with someone in a hard first line? Day four hundred seventeen.

If you could ask for one thing. Not three wishes. Not a list. One. What would it be? Most of us would struggle. Health, probably. For the people we love to be safe. Money, a little more of it. For the diagnosis to be wrong. For the person who left to come back. Now picture someone surrounded: enemies closing in, an army camped around, false witnesses lining up, and he even imagines his own father and mother turning away. If anyone has a long list of requests, it's him. And then he says: I've asked for one thing. Only one.
screen: `IF YOU COULD ASK FOR ONE THING.` → `SURROUNDED, WITH A LONG LIST.` → `ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: Psalm twenty-seven opens, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Two questions, and they're not quite rhetorical. The psalmist knows exactly whom he could fear. He names them: evildoers, a host encamped against him, war rising up. The fear is real. The questions are his way of standing up inside it. Then, the one thing: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple." Not rescue first. Not victory. Nearness. To live close to God, and to look at his beauty. Everything else, the psalm seems to say, follows from that one thing, or matters less without it. The psalm doesn't pretend the fear goes away all at once. Halfway through it swings back to pleading: hide not thy face from me. Then the most tender line: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up." And it ends not with a victory but with waiting: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." Twice. Wait. A few things worth knowing. Jewish communities recite Psalm twenty-seven every day for weeks around the High Holy Days in the fall. And the first words, in Latin, Dominus illuminatio mea, the Lord is my light, have been the motto of the University of Oxford for centuries.
screen: `TWO QUESTIONS, ASKED INSIDE FEAR.` · `ONE THING: TO DWELL NEAR.` · `WHEN MY FATHER AND MOTHER FORSAKE ME.` · `WAIT, AND BE OF GOOD COURAGE.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY LIGHT; WHOM SHALL I FEAR?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the one thing you'd ask. Settle, and breathe. Let your list of wants come up: all of it, the big and the small. Don't fight it. Then begin setting things down, one by one, like taking items out of an overfull bag. Keep going until you're holding one thing. Just one. It may surprise you. It may be close to the psalmist's, or something else entirely. Hold it. If you pray, you can ask God for it plainly. If you don't, just let yourself know what it is. The bell holds the time.
Whom shall I fear? The question that opens Psalm twenty-seven, asked from inside real danger by someone whose light is God.
Your line: one thing I ask. Today, when you catch yourself wanting ten things at once, come back to your one. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: Joy in the morning (Psalm 30)
418.hook: weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning
418.howItsDone: Christians often pray Psalm 30 at Easter and in times of recovery and thanksgiving, and its line 'joy cometh in the morning' is often said at funerals and hospital bedsides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm twenty-seven: the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear? Your line was one thing I ask. Did you come back to your one thing? Day four hundred eighteen.

Everybody knows the long night. Lying awake with a fever. Sitting in a hospital waiting room as the clock crawls past three. The night after a breakup, or bad news, or a fight you can't take back. Everything feels heavier in the dark. Worries grow teeth. And then, sometimes without anything at all being fixed, the window goes gray, then pale, and a bird starts up outside, and the same problem looks different in daylight. Not solved. Just survivable. One psalm puts that whole experience into a single line, and it's become one of the best-known lines in the Psalms.
screen: `EVERYBODY KNOWS THE LONG NIGHT.` → `WORRIES GROW TEETH IN THE DARK.` → `THEN THE WINDOW GOES GRAY.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty, in the King James Bible: "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." The Hebrew picture is even more vivid. The word for endure, yalin, means to lodge, to spend the night. Weeping comes in like an overnight guest. It's allowed in. It stays the night. But it doesn't move in. In the morning, joy arrives, and the guest leaves. The psalm is a thank-you, and it tells a story. The writer says that when things were going well, he got comfortable. "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved." Then God hid his face, he says, and he was troubled. He fell ill, or nearly died; he talks about going down to the pit. He cried out. And he was healed. And then the line that makes people dance: "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness." Sackcloth was the rough cloth people wore in grief. God, the psalm says, took it off him like a parent changing a child's clothes, and dressed him in joy. The heading calls it a song for the dedication of the house, and nobody is quite sure which house. In Jewish prayer it opens the morning psalms each day, and it's linked with Hanukkah, the feast of the temple's rededication. Christians have long prayed it at Easter. The psalm doesn't say the night isn't real. It says the night isn't permanent.
screen: `WEEPING STAYS THE NIGHT, LIKE A GUEST.` · `I SAID, I SHALL NEVER BE MOVED.` · `MOURNING TURNED INTO DANCING.` · `THE NIGHT IS NOT PERMANENT.` · then, large: `WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the morning light. If it's morning where you are, look at it now: where it falls in the room, its color, how it moves. If it's later, find whatever light there is, a lamp, a window, a screen dimmed low, and picture tomorrow's first light coming. Settle, and breathe. Think of one night in your life that felt endless, and that ended. You got through it. Let yourself feel that. If you're in a long night now, you don't have to feel joy yet. Just remember that mornings come. If you pray, you can give thanks for one morning. The bell holds the time.
Joy in the morning. From Psalm thirty: weeping may stay the night like a guest, but joy comes in the morning.
Your line: joy comes in the morning. Tomorrow, before you check anything, look at the first light for ten seconds. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: When I kept silent (Psalm 32)
419.hook: holding a wrong in, my bones wasted away; confessing, I was forgiven
419.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess in the sacrament of reconciliation; many Protestants confess privately to God or in prayers of confession in worship. Psalm 32 is one of the seven penitential psalms, often prayed in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty: weeping stays the night like a guest. Your line was joy comes in the morning. Did you catch the first light? Day four hundred nineteen.

You said something sharp to a friend three weeks ago. Or you took credit for something that wasn't quite yours. Or you told a small lie, and then another to cover it. Nobody found out. Nobody's asking. And yet. It sits there. You feel it when their name comes up. You feel it at night, in your shoulders, in your stomach. It's strange how something so small, held in, can get so heavy. Long ago, someone felt exactly that, and wrote it down in a psalm that's almost a medical chart of a guilty conscience.
screen: `SOMETHING SMALL, NEVER SAID.` → `IT SITS IN YOUR SHOULDERS.` → `A CHART OF A GUILTY CONSCIENCE.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-two starts at the end of the story, with relief, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." Then it goes back and tells how it got there. "When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer." Look at the body in those lines. Bones aging. Groaning all day. Dried out, like a field in August. The silence wasn't peaceful. It was exhausting. Holding the thing in took everything he had. And then the turn, and it happens fast: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." One sentence. I said I will confess, and you forgave. The weight he carried for who knows how long lifts in a single breath. Then God speaks: "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye." And a gentle warning: don't be like a horse or a mule that has to be steered with a bit and bridle. Christians have treasured this psalm. Paul quotes its opening in his letter to the Romans. The church counts it among the seven penitential psalms. And Augustine's biographer says that when he was dying, Augustine had the penitential psalms copied and put on the wall where he could read them from his bed. Christians practice confession differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest in a sacrament. Many Protestants confess directly to God, and some to a trusted friend. All of them know the weight of the silence.
screen: `IT STARTS WITH RELIEF.` · `SILENCE DRIED ME OUT.` · `I SAID I WILL, AND THOU FORGAVEST.` · `NOT LIKE A HORSE OR A MULE.` · then, large: `WHEN I KEPT SILENCE, MY BONES WAXED OLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: confess one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Let one small wrong come to mind, something you've been carrying in silence. Not the biggest thing. A small one. Notice where you feel it in your body. Then say it, plainly. If you pray, say it to God, in your own words, just as it is. If you don't, say it out loud to the empty room, or write it on a piece of paper. Then notice your shoulders. If there's someone you need to say it to, picture yourself doing it, soon. The bell holds the time.
When I kept silent. Psalm thirty-two's picture of a wrong held in: bones aging, strength dried up, until one honest sentence brought forgiveness.
Your line: silence was heavy. Today, say the small thing you've been holding, to God, to yourself, or to the person who needs to hear it. Day four hundred nineteen.

420.title: Taste and see (Psalm 34)
420.hook: O taste and see that the Lord is good
420.howItsDone: Many churches, Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and others, sing 'O taste and see' during communion, a custom described as early as Cyril of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-two: when I kept silent, my bones waxed old. Your line was silence was heavy. Did you say the small thing? Day four hundred twenty, the end of week sixty.

You can read a whole cookbook about peaches. Their varieties, their season, the chemistry of their sugars, the best way to tell when one's ripe. You can become an expert. And then someone hands you a real one, warm from the tree, and you bite into it, and the juice runs down your wrist, and in two seconds you know something the whole book couldn't tell you. Some knowledge only comes through the mouth. One psalm takes that ordinary truth and turns it into an invitation, and it's been sung in churches for more than sixteen hundred years at one particular moment.

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-four, in the King James Bible: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Taste first, then see. Not see first, and maybe taste later if the evidence is good enough. The psalm puts experience before understanding. You come to know God's goodness, it says, the way you know a peach: by trying it. And this isn't a psalm of easy times. The heading ties it to a story about David running for his life, pretending to be mad in front of a foreign king so he'd be let go. A detail worth knowing: the heading names the king Abimelech, while the story in the book of Samuel calls him Achish. Scholars have different explanations; the sources don't settle it. Either way, this is a song from someone who escaped by the skin of his teeth. "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears." And one of its best-known lines: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." Near the brokenhearted. Not the strong. The psalm is also an acrostic: in Hebrew, its verses run roughly through the alphabet, one letter after another, like a child's ABC of trust. And here's where the taste comes in for many Christians. In the fourth century, Cyril of Jerusalem described the newly baptized hearing a singer chant this verse as they came forward to receive communion: taste and see. Many churches still sing it at the Lord's table. And what a week it's been: pleasant places, the heavens declaring, my God my God, whom shall I fear, joy in the morning, the heavy silence, and now, a taste.
screen: `TASTE FIRST, THEN SEE.` · `A SONG OF A NARROW ESCAPE.` · `NIGH UNTO THE BROKEN HEART.` · `SUNG AT COMMUNION SINCE CYRIL.` · then, large: `O TASTE AND SEE THAT THE LORD IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: taste your food slowly. If you have something to eat or drink nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a sip of tea, take it now. If not, save this for your next meal. Settle, and breathe. Put one small bite in your mouth and don't chew yet. Notice the texture, the temperature. Then chew slowly, and notice the flavor arrive, change, and fade. Swallow, and notice the aftertaste. You've just learned something no description could teach you. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Taste and see. Psalm thirty-four's invitation to know God's goodness by experience, like tasting food, and a verse long sung at communion.

Your line: taste and see. Today, eat one meal, or one bite, slowly, without a screen. And that's week sixty: pleasant places, the heavens, my God, light, morning, silence, and a taste. Day four hundred twenty.
